identity.title: WebDevJudge: Evaluating (M)LLMs as Critiques for Web Development Quality

problem.claim: Assess whether LLMs and related evaluators can reliably judge web-development quality.

gap.claim: Reliability of LLM-as-a-judge for open-ended tasks involving dynamic environments and complex interactions remains unexplored.

contributions.claim: Introduces WebDevJudge, a systematic benchmark supporting static, non-interactive and dynamic, continuous interactive evaluation.
Provides human preferences over paired web implementations with structured, query-grounded rubrics.
Evaluates LLMs, MLLMs, and agentic workflows across evaluation paradigms and guidance mechanisms.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish WebDevJudge by combining static-observation and continuous interactive evaluation for web development.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report a significant gap between LLM judges and human experts.
The authors attribute this gap to failures in recognizing functional equivalence, verifying task feasibility, and mitigating bias.

narrative_sequence.summary: LLM-as-a-judge is presented as a scalable alternative to human evaluation for well-defined tasks.
The abstract identifies uncertainty about reliability in open-ended, dynamic, interactive settings.
WebDevJudge combines static and interactive web-environment evaluation with rubric-grounded human preference labels.
The benchmark is used to compare LLMs, MLLMs, and agentic workflows under different paradigms and guidance mechanisms.
The authors report a substantial human–model judging gap and connect it to specific capability and bias failures.

source_observation.claim: The abstract separates static observation from continuous interaction and links the reported judging gap to concrete failure modes.

lessons.interpretation: A benchmark can make difficult evaluation settings and hypothesized failure mechanisms explicit rather than treating quality judgment as a single capability.
lessons.application: When proposing an evaluator study, define distinct environment-interaction modes and map aggregate results to diagnostic error categories.
lessons.exception: This structure may be unsuitable when the target task has no meaningful dynamic state or when failure modes cannot be operationalized from available observations.

unknowns: The abstract gives no benchmark size, task distribution, evaluator identities, metrics, guidance details, or magnitude of the reported gap.
The claim that rubrics ensure high-quality ground truth is author-reported; annotator procedures and agreement are unspecified.
The abstract does not report whether any evaluator or guidance mechanism improved performance.
